description: Width tiers for Year 2 English — all 27 ACARA v9 descriptors. Generated from elaborations using width_generation_prompt v1.0.
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement that genuinely meets the descriptor's command term. For concept/language descriptors (LA, LE): the narrowest context or phenomenon that still satisfies the command term. For capability descriptors (LY literacy mode B): the simplest task type in which the capability is demonstrated.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects sound standard practice without requiring every elaboration to be covered.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add contexts, phenomena or task types. For language/concept descriptors: more contexts or cultural examples. For capability descriptors: more task types or application contexts. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are source data. They are examples of how the descriptor might be addressed, not a required checklist. Some elaborations represent the same phenomenon at different specificity — these are merged.

AC9E2LA01.minimum_width: Identify how language changes between two contrasting contexts — e.g. greeting a friend vs a teacher — and name the contextual difference that drives the change.
AC9E2LA01.typical_width: Investigate how language choices vary across multiple contexts (formal/informal, familiar/unfamiliar) and roles (speaker, listener, questioner, instruction-giver); explore culturally specific greetings and expressions of politeness across at least two cultural contexts.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian cultural protocols in Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country, examining how role (greeter, guest, witness) shapes language choices
Investigate how familiarity with a group or individual influences language choices across a range of community and school contexts
Compare greeting and politeness conventions from two different cultural backgrounds and discuss what values each reflects
elaborations: exploring culturally specific greetings and expressions of politeness
exploring First Nations Australian cultural protocols in Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country, and the greeting words used by local First Nations Australians
exploring how familiarity with a group or individual influences language choices

AC9E2LA02.minimum_width: Use an appreciation sentence that names a specific textual feature (e.g. 'I liked how the author described the setting because …') and identify at least one preference verb.
AC9E2LA02.typical_width: Explore how appreciation language names specific textual features across multiple texts; use a range of preference verbs (liked, preferred, enjoyed) to express degree; discuss how specific vocabulary — including topic-relevant language — makes appreciation more precise.
wider: Identify First Nations Australian language words specific to Country/Place used in texts and discuss how they enable more specific appreciation of setting
Compare appreciation statements using general vs specific vocabulary and discuss the effect on the reader
Explore appreciation language used in published book reviews or reader responses and identify the features they reference
elaborations: exploring how language is used to appreciate texts using more precise vocabulary; for example, 'I liked how the author described the setting because …'
exploring verbs used to express degree of preference; for example, 'liked', 'preferred', 'enjoyed'
identifying First Nations Australian language words specific to Country/Place that help the reader to be specific when appreciating the setting in a text

AC9E2LA03.minimum_width: Identify the purpose of two different text types and name one structural feature that serves each purpose.
AC9E2LA03.typical_width: Identify the organisation and language features in narratives, recounts, information reports, simple procedures, expressions of opinion and responses to texts; discuss how each text type's features serve its purpose; recognise that the same purpose can take different forms.
wider: Compare two texts with the same purpose but different forms (e.g. opinion as poster vs email vs brochure) and discuss how the form shapes language and layout
Identify texts from other curriculum areas (Science report, HASS recount) and compare their structural features with English text types
Investigate how digital text types (infographic, ebook, website) use organisational features differently from print equivalents
elaborations: identifying the typical features of a text; for example, a typical introduction to a narrative or the use of dot points in instructions
identifying that different types of texts might have different forms; for example, an expression of opinion might be in the form of a poster, email or brochure

identifying the organisation and language features in texts such as narratives, recounts, information reports, simple procedures, expression of opinion and responses to texts (including poetry), and discuss their purposes

AC9E2LA04.minimum_width: Identify the referent of a personal pronoun in a sentence and identify one instance of ellipsis and what can be inferred.
AC9E2LA04.typical_width: Track pronoun reference chains across paragraphs in both narrative and informative texts; map word associations for a character or entity; identify and explain instances of ellipsis across multiple text types.
wider: Identify ambiguous pronoun reference in texts and discuss how broader context resolves or fails to resolve the ambiguity
Compare ellipsis in dialogue vs narration in a picture book and discuss why dialogue uses more ellipsis
Compare first-person and third-person narrative pronoun chains and discuss how each affects the reader's relationship to the story
elaborations: identifying language used to build information across a text
mapping examples of word associations in texts; for example, words that refer to the main character
tracking how a person or thing is identified through a section of a text
identifying words left out that can be inferred from the surrounding text
using personal and possessive pronouns to link entities previously mentioned in the text

AC9E2LA05.minimum_width: Use a table of contents or index to locate specific information in a print text, and use a navigation menu or link to locate specific information on a digital text.
AC9E2LA05.typical_width: Navigate print texts using chapters, tables of contents and indexes; navigate digital texts using side-bar menus, drop-down menus and links; explain how each navigation tool is organised to support information retrieval.
wider: Compare information retrieval using a print index vs a website search for the same topic, discussing efficiency and accuracy trade-offs
Compare navigation structures of two different websites with similar purposes and evaluate which is easier to use
Explore how navigation tools change between mobile and desktop versions of the same digital text
elaborations: recognising how numbered chapters, organisation of tables of content and alphabetical order of indexes operate to support access to information
exploring how the navigation tools of different websites can be used to locate information

AC9E2LA06.minimum_width: Identify that a compound sentence contains two independent clauses and correctly name the coordinating conjunction linking them.
AC9E2LA06.typical_width: Identify, construct and use compound sentences with 'and', 'but' and 'so'; explain the relationship each conjunction signals; use compound sentences flexibly in short writing tasks.
wider: Experiment with three-clause compound sentences and discuss the rhythmic and emphatic effects
Compare the effect of substituting one conjunction for another in a compound sentence and discuss how meaning changes
Identify compound sentences in shared reading texts and evaluate whether the conjunction chosen is the best option
elaborations: using coordinating conjunctions; for example, 'and', 'but', 'so' to construct compound sentences
AC9E2LA06.width_notes: This descriptor has one elaboration. Wider items are inferred from the descriptor's scope, which is consistent with typical Year 2 English grammar teaching.

AC9E2LA07.minimum_width: Identify a noun group (head noun + article + adjective) and a verb group (main verb + auxiliary) in given sentences.
AC9E2LA07.typical_width: Build extended noun groups using articles and adjectives by applying the 'how many?', 'what type?', 'what's it like?' questioning scaffold; identify and build verb groups using auxiliaries; analyse both in sentences across multiple text types.
wider: Compare noun group density across different text types — sparse in procedures, rich in narratives — and discuss why each text type uses them as it does
Compare active and passive verb groups ('touched' vs 'was touched') and discuss the effect on who is foregrounded
Build extended noun groups for cross-curriculum vocabulary (e.g. Science, HASS) and discuss how each element adds information
elaborations: identifying nouns that refer to people, places, concrete objects and ideas in sentences in texts, and identifying the articles and adjectives that extend those nouns
building extended noun groups using articles and adjectives; for example, 'the longest side'
building extended verb groups using verbs; for example, 'was touched'
investigating how noun groups can be built up by asking questions about the noun such as 'how many?', 'what's it like?', 'what type?'

AC9E2LA08.minimum_width: Identify one image that adds information not in the written text and one image that amplifies meaning that the words express.
AC9E2LA08.typical_width: Identify and discuss multiple instances of images adding meaning and images multiplying meaning across factual and narrative texts; analyse how characters' visual representations add to or extend the written narrative.
wider: Compare a text with images to the same text with images removed and discuss what meaning is lost or changed
Identify images whose meaning is ironic or contradictory relative to the words — where the image complicates rather than confirms the written text
Compare image-text relationships across different text types (picture book, infographic, digital news) and discuss how each uses images differently
elaborations: identifying images and graphics in a text that add ideas or information not included in the written text
identifying visual representations of characters' actions, reactions, speech and thought processes in narratives, and considering how these images add to or multiply the meaning of accompanying words

AC9E2LA09.minimum_width: Replace one everyday word with a topic-specific alternative in a given sentence and explain the improvement in precision.
AC9E2LA09.typical_width: Experiment with vocabulary choices across multiple topics — Science, HASS, English — replacing everyday language with topic-specific alternatives; explore character-description vocabulary in narratives; make at least two deliberate vocabulary choices during editing.
wider: Identify First Nations Australians' language words relevant to a topic being studied and discuss what they communicate that English vocabulary does not
Compare the vocabulary used for the same topic in texts aimed at different audiences (children vs adult) and discuss how audience shapes vocabulary choices
Use a vocabulary journal from a current learning area topic to deliberately draw on when writing
elaborations: selecting vocabulary appropriate to the topic to replace everyday language
discussing new vocabulary encountered in learning area texts
exploring language used to describe characters in narratives, including nouns and adjectives
identifying words from First Nations Australians' languages relevant to a topic

AC9E2LA10.minimum_width: Identify capital letters in the title of a text and commas separating items in a list, and explain the function of each.
AC9E2LA10.typical_width: Identify capital letter usage in titles across multiple text types; identify commas in lists across a variety of texts including classroom, informative and narrative contexts; distinguish title capitalisation from sentence-start capitalisation.
wider: Compare capitalisation conventions across different title styles (all words vs content words vs first word only) and identify which texts use each
Identify titles and lists in digital texts and compare their conventions with print text equivalents
Explore how comma usage in lists prevents ambiguity by comparing punctuated and unpunctuated versions of the same list
elaborations: identifying how capital letters are used in the titles of texts
identifying commas used in lists in a variety of types of texts

AC9E2LE01.minimum_width: Identify one character-setting connection in a text from any of the three author groups (First Nations Australian, Australian, world) and explain the connection.
AC9E2LE01.typical_width: Discuss character-setting connections across texts from First Nations Australian, wide-ranging Australian and world authors; identify recurring character-setting patterns in different literary traditions; discuss how the Australian outback or specific Country shapes characters and stories.
wider: Compare the same character archetype (e.g. wise elder, lost child) in texts from at least two different cultural or national traditions and discuss how the setting shapes the character differently
Compare how the same geographical setting is depicted by a First Nations Australian author vs a non-First Nations author, discussing differences in the character-place relationship
Explore how illustrators from different cultural backgrounds depict settings and characters and discuss the visual conventions each uses
elaborations: discussing the depiction of characters in particular settings in well-known fairytales from wide-ranging world authors
recognising recurring characters in particular settings in texts by First Nations Australian authors
exploring the way wide-ranging Australian authors and illustrators depict the Australian outback and the associated characters

AC9E2LE02.strand: Engaging with and responding to literature
AC9E2LE02.minimum_width: Identify one literary feature (character, setting) in a text and give a reasoned explanation for a preference that references that feature.
AC9E2LE02.typical_width: Identify features across multiple texts and give reasoned preference explanations; discuss preferences for familiar vs unfamiliar worlds, and for characters with similar or different lives; respond to non-human characters' behaviours.
wider: Discuss preferences for texts with morally complex characters — those whose behaviour is a mix of positive and negative — and explain what makes them compelling
Compare preferences within a class for the same text, discussing how different readers respond to different features
Evaluate preferences across a collection of texts read over a unit, identifying patterns in what features consistently create strong responses
elaborations: discussing preferences for stories set in familiar or unfamiliar worlds, or about characters whose lives are like or unlike their own
discussing their feelings about the positive and negative behaviours of non-human characters, such as animals

AC9E2LE03.minimum_width: Identify one language feature used to describe a character and one used to describe a setting in a given text, and explain what each contributes.
AC9E2LE03.typical_width: Identify and discuss language used to describe characters and settings across multiple texts; compare how different authors present similar character types or settings using different language choices; discuss the different effects produced.
wider: Compare language used to describe hero and villain characters in the same text, discussing how word choices position the reader
Compare how the same type of setting is described by two different authors from different cultural contexts and discuss what the difference reveals
Identify language in texts by First Nations Australian authors that describes relationships between characters and Country, and discuss how it differs from other setting language
elaborations: identifying language used to describe characters' appearance and personality in different texts
identifying language features used to create a sense of place

AC9E2LE04.minimum_width: Identify the rhythmic pattern in a simple poem or chant and reproduce it with reasonable accuracy.
AC9E2LE04.typical_width: Identify, reproduce and experiment with rhythmic patterns across poems, chants, rhymes and songs; create an original two-line rhythmic sequence using a deliberate sound pattern; explore how word sounds create effects for an audience.
wider: Create a new verse for an existing poem that maintains the original rhythmic pattern
Compare rhythmic patterns from chants used in different cultural contexts (ceremony, play, sport) and discuss how rhythm serves each purpose
Invent nonsense words using known sound patterns and discuss how sound creates meaning even without semantic content
elaborations: experimenting with syllables and sounds to create new words and names in poems
exploring how poets use word sounds to create effects for an audience

AC9E2LE05.minimum_width: Create a short imaginative text or adaptation with an identifiable character, setting and narrative structure.
AC9E2LE05.typical_width: Create imaginative texts or adaptations using key literary features deliberately — character with specific language, setting that connects to character, narrative structure with orientation/complication/resolution; review and revise the text.
wider: Create an adaptation that moves a familiar character into a different setting and explore how the new setting changes the character's behaviour and the plot
Create a narrative where the complication arises directly from the character-setting relationship
Create an imaginative text in a form other than prose — poem, storyboard, script — using the same key literary features
elaborations: creating texts that include characters and settings
creating adaptations of texts changing characters or settings
creating new narrative endings or episodes

AC9E2LY01.minimum_width: Name two different text types that present the same topic and identify one difference in how the information is presented.
AC9E2LY01.typical_width: Identify and compare how a topic is presented across three or more text types — e.g. poem, narrative and information report on lifecycles — discussing what each type emphasises and why.
wider: Explore a practical topic (e.g. recipes) presented in food packets, recipe books, short videos and digital apps — comparing shared purpose with different forms
Identify a cross-curriculum topic and find examples from multiple text types, discussing what each adds to understanding of the topic
Compare how a poem and an information report about the same topic use language differently and discuss why
elaborations: reading a poem, narrative and informative text about lifecycles and discussing what is learnt
exploring recipes presented on food packets, in recipe books, in short video clips and in a digital form, noting their shared purpose

AC9E2LY02.minimum_width: Demonstrate active listening by paraphrasing a partner's contribution; express an opinion using a sentence starter; respond to another's opinion respectfully.
AC9E2LY02.typical_width: Use a range of interaction skills across different discussion contexts — think-pair-share, class discussion, small group — including active listening, expressing and responding to opinions, giving instructions, asking clarifying questions, and using strategies to disagree respectfully.
wider: Lead a short structured discussion using a roles framework (facilitator, timekeeper, recorder) and debrief on which interaction skills were used
Compare the interaction patterns in a structured debate vs an exploratory discussion and discuss how the purpose shapes the required skills
Identify and reflect on a discussion that broke down — discussing what interaction skill was missing and how it could be repaired
elaborations: exploring ways to comment on what others say using sentence starters
demonstrating appropriate listening behaviours, responding to and paraphrasing a partner's contribution
asking relevant questions and making connections with personal experiences and the contributions of others
understanding how to disagree or respectfully offer an alternative

AC9E2LY03.minimum_width: Identify the purpose and intended audience of one imaginative, one informative and one persuasive text.
AC9E2LY03.typical_width: Identify purpose and audience across a range of text types including advertisements, signs and texts by First Nations Australian authors; explain how text features signal both purpose and audience.
wider: Compare two versions of information aimed at different audiences (e.g. children's vs adult's book on same topic) and identify what features change for each audience
Analyse the audience assumptions embedded in an advertisement — discussing what the creator assumed about who would see it and respond to it
Identify texts by First Nations Australian authors and discuss how their purposes may include cultural preservation, community address or sharing knowledge of Country
elaborations: identifying the purpose of texts written by First Nations Australian authors
identifying the audience of advertisements and signs

AC9E2LY04.minimum_width: Apply a decoding strategy when encountering an unfamiliar word; identify a point where meaning breaks down and re-read to self-correct.
AC9E2LY04.typical_width: Read texts with phrasing and fluency, applying phonic, morphemic and sight-word knowledge to decode; monitor comprehension and self-correct spontaneously; re-read sections when meaning is lost.
wider: Read texts with increasing decoding complexity (compound words, silent letters, less common vowel patterns) applying appropriate strategies
Analyse a self-corrected reading error and identify which cue was used to detect and fix it
Compare the experience of reading with and without active monitoring — discussing what comprehension is lost when monitoring is passive
elaborations: using phonic (sound–letter) and morphemic knowledge, and knowledge of high-frequency words when decoding text
monitoring own reading, self-correcting or reading back, re-reading when meaning does not make sense

AC9E2LY05.minimum_width: Make one prediction supported by a text cue; make one inference integrating at least two information sources; identify the main idea of a text.
AC9E2LY05.typical_width: Apply visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning strategies across informative and persuasive texts; make inferences by integrating print, images and prior knowledge; use graphic organisers to represent connections.
wider: Compare inferences made by different readers about the same text and discuss why they differ and which is better supported
Apply comprehension strategies to a text from another curriculum area and discuss how content knowledge supports inference
Use a structured reading protocol (e.g. predict-read-confirm) across a whole text and reflect on which strategies were most useful
elaborations: listening for specific information and providing key facts from an informative or persuasive text
integrating information from print, images and prior knowledge to make supportable inferences
identifying the main idea of a text
predicting vocabulary likely to be in a text based on topic and purpose
using prior knowledge to make and confirm predictions when reading
using graphic organisers to represent connections between characters, events or information

AC9E2LY06.minimum_width: Create a short written text for a familiar audience with an appropriate structure, at least one compound sentence, and one deliberate vocabulary choice.
AC9E2LY06.typical_width: Create and edit imaginative, informative and persuasive texts using appropriate structures, simple and compound sentences, extended noun groups and verb groups, topic-specific vocabulary, simple punctuation and common two-syllable words; edit for vocabulary precision and grammatical accuracy.
wider: Create a multimodal text that integrates written and visual elements, making deliberate decisions about what each mode carries
Annotate an edited draft explaining the changes made and why each improves the text
Create the same text in two different text types (e.g. an informative text as a report and as an infographic) and discuss how the form changes the language choices
elaborations: creating written texts so that readers follow the sequence of ideas or events
using vocabulary, including topic-specific vocabulary, appropriate to the purpose
using digital tools to create texts
using simple and compound sentences correctly and flexibly
editing by adding, deleting or changing vocabulary to improve a text
reviewing sentences for grammatical accuracy

AC9E2LY07.minimum_width: Plan and deliver a short oral presentation with an appropriate structure, at least two topic-specific vocabulary items, and one deliberate variation in tone, volume or pace.
AC9E2LY07.typical_width: Create, rehearse and deliver presentations across different purposes — informative and persuasive — using appropriate structures and topic-specific vocabulary, varying tone, volume and pace; adjust for more formal delivery contexts.
wider: Deliver the same content with two different delivery styles (formal vs informal) and discuss the effect on the audience
Record and review a rehearsal, identifying specific delivery improvements; implement changes and compare recordings
Deliver a multimodal presentation integrating digital or visual elements with oral delivery, coordinating the two modes
elaborations: preparing and delivering oral presentations using more formal language and specific vocabulary about content area topics
sequencing ideas, points or events appropriately
adjusting volume and tone when speaking in more formal situations

AC9E2LY08.minimum_width: Write a short passage with all letters correctly formed, legible, and using consistent unjoined upper- and lower-case letterforms.
AC9E2LY08.typical_width: Write across varied tasks with growing fluency — letter formation is consistent and does not slow composition; functional pencil grip maintained throughout.
wider: Limited width — legible handwriting with growing fluency is a developmental capacity built through practice volume rather than breadth of contexts. Extensions such as increasing writing speed or reducing inter-letter variability go further in one dimension rather than broadening the skill across new contexts.
elaborations: consolidating a functional pencil grip/grasp
AC9E2LY08.width_notes: Thin width acknowledged — this is a fluency-building descriptor with one elaboration. Width is narrow; consolidation through practice volume is the appropriate teacher investment signal.

AC9E2LY09.minimum_width: Blend and segment a word with a complex phoneme cluster; delete or substitute a phoneme at a specified position to form a new word.
AC9E2LY09.typical_width: Apply blending, segmenting, deletion and substitution to a range of words with complex phoneme patterns — multi-consonant clusters, medial digraphs — at initial, medial and final positions; connect spoken manipulation to reading and writing new words.
wider: Generate word families through systematic phoneme substitution at a single position and discuss what the pattern reveals
Apply phoneme manipulation to decode new words encountered during reading rather than only in isolated practice
Compare segmentation of words with similar-sounding clusters (e.g. 'scratch' vs 'catch') and discuss how spelling relates to the sounds
elaborations: blending and segmenting sounds in words; for example, 'b-r-o-th-er' or 'c-l-ou-d-y'
deleting and substituting sounds in spoken words to form new words

AC9E2LY10.minimum_width: Correctly read and write words with common vowel digraphs; read a word with a silent letter or less common long vowel pattern; decode a two-syllable word syllable by syllable.
AC9E2LY10.typical_width: Apply vowel digraph, less common long vowel pattern, silent letter and consonant cluster knowledge when reading and writing words of one or more syllables including compound words; apply decoding strategies syllable-by-syllable.
wider: Compare vowel digraphs with the same sound but different spelling (e.g. 'ee' and 'ea') and discuss strategies for choosing the correct spelling
Identify compound words in learning area texts, decompose them into constituents, and discuss how the parts contribute to word meaning
Identify silent letter patterns across word families (e.g. 'kn-' words: knife, knot, know) and discuss the pattern
elaborations: reading words with digraphs where one letter is not pronounced
providing the sounds for less common letter–sound matches; for example, 'ight'
reading words with vowel digraphs ('ee', 'oo', 'ai', 'ay', 'ea')

AC9E2LY11.minimum_width: Correctly spell at least three irregular high-frequency words in writing; use a known word to spell an unknown word by morphemic analogy.
AC9E2LY11.typical_width: Apply spelling pattern and morphemic knowledge to read and write a range of words with unpredictable sound-spelling relationships; use context to select the correct form for words with more than one plausible pronunciation.
wider: Build word families from irregular base words (e.g. 'one', 'once', 'only', 'lone') and discuss what the morphemic relationships reveal
Apply morphemic knowledge to spell unknown words encountered in cross-curriculum reading and writing
Group irregular words by shared spelling pattern and discuss what the patterns suggest about English spelling history
elaborations: using known words and knowledge of spelling patterns and morphemes to write unknown words; for example, 'one', 'once', 'only' and 'lone'
using context to read the correct word when an unknown word has more than one plausible pronunciation

AC9E2LY12.minimum_width: Build at least three words in a family from a known base word using at least one prefix and one suffix.
AC9E2LY12.typical_width: Build morphemic word families from several base words using a range of prefixes and suffixes; apply morphemic knowledge to spell unknown words by analogy; distinguish meaning-changing prefixes from grammatical suffixes.
wider: Map a complex word family (e.g. 'cover' → cover, uncover, covering, covered, recover, discovery) and discuss how each affix changes meaning or function
Use morphemic knowledge from a known word to decode and spell new words encountered in learning area reading
Compare how the same prefix (e.g. 'un-') operates across different base words and identify what it consistently contributes to meaning
elaborations: using morphemic knowledge of words to spell unknown words; for example, 'one', 'once', 'cover', 'covering', 'uncover'
writing unknown words using morphemic knowledge; for example, using the known word 'friend' to write 'friendly' and 'friendship'
